meta.titre: Earth Movements and Seasons: defining solstice, equinox, rotation and revolution, and spotting false causes
meta.sous_theme: Rotation, revolution, solstices, equinoxes and the true cause of the seasons

sections.contenu_markdown: In Douala the sun rises at almost the same time all year, yet a cousin in Paris writes that the evenings in June are light until late and the days in December are very short. Students often think this is because Paris moves closer to the Sun in summer. The GCE paper likes to test exactly this belief with a multiple-choice question, and to ask for short definitions of the Earth's movements. Once you can separate the true causes from the false ones, these marks become easy to win.

items: The Earth is a sphere that spins on an imaginary line through the North Pole and the South Pole called the axis.
The Tropic of Cancer is at 23.5°N, the equator at 0° and the Tropic of Capricorn at 23.5°S.
The Sun gives out light and heat, and rays that strike the ground more directly heat it more.

sections.titre: The two movements of the Earth, the tilted axis and the key dates of the year
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Four terms to define exactly
| Term | Meaning | Main result |
|---|---|---|
| Rotation | The spinning of the Earth on its axis, from west to east, in about 24 hours | Day and night, and differences in clock time between places |
| Revolution | The movement of the Earth along its path round the Sun, taking about 365¼ days | The seasons and the changing length of day and night |
| Solstice | The date when the overhead Sun is at its furthest point north or south of the equator, at a tropic | Longest day in one hemisphere and shortest day in the other |
| Equinox | The date when the overhead Sun is on the equator | Day and night equal in length all over the world |

### The real cause of the seasons
The Earth's axis is tilted by 23.5° from the vertical. During the whole revolution the axis points in the same direction in space. So for part of the year the Northern Hemisphere leans towards the Sun and for the other part the Southern Hemisphere does. The hemisphere leaning towards the Sun receives more direct rays and longer days, so it is warmer: it has summer. The other hemisphere has winter at the same time.

### Dates to know
| Date (about) | Event | Overhead Sun |
|---|---|---|
| 21 March | Equinox | Equator |
| 21 June | Solstice | Tropic of Cancer (23.5°N) |
| 23 September | Equinox | Equator |
| 22 December | Solstice | Tropic of Capricorn (23.5°S) |

### Causes and non-causes
True causes: the tilt of the axis, the constant direction of the axis, and revolution round the Sun. Not causes: rotation (it gives day and night, not seasons), the distance from the Sun (the Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January, when the Northern Hemisphere has winter), the phases of the Moon, or the speed of the wind.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the command word is define, state or briefly explain what a term means
variantes.contenu_markdown: Give one clear sentence per term and add its effect or date if marks allow. Keep the pairs apart: rotation is the spin on the axis, revolution is the journey round the Sun; a solstice is an extreme position of the overhead Sun at a tropic, an equinox is the overhead Sun on the equator.

variantes.nom: Identify the item that is not a cause
variantes.quand_utiliser: When a multiple-choice question asks which statement does not explain the seasons
variantes.contenu_markdown: Test every option against the three true causes (tilt, constant direction of the axis, revolution). Any option that mentions the Earth's distance from the Sun, the speed of rotation or the Moon is the odd one out. Read the word NOT before you choose, and cross out options you know are true causes.

variantes.nom: Where the tropics and the polar circles come from
variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question links the tilt to latitude lines or to the height of the Sun
variantes.contenu_markdown: The tropics lie at the same number of degrees as the tilt, 23.5°. The polar circles lie at $90° - 23.5° = 66.5°$. At noon the Sun's angle above the horizon equals $90°$ minus the number of degrees between your latitude and the latitude of the overhead Sun. Between the two tropics, a place has the overhead Sun twice a year.

sections.enonce_markdown: (a) Name two effects of rotation and two effects of revolution. (b) A student writes that August is hot in Europe because the Earth moves nearer to the Sun. Explain why this is wrong and give the correct reason.

etapes.action: Separate the two movements before listing effects.
etapes.justification: Examiners give marks only when each effect is attached to the right movement.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Rotation (spin on the axis in about 24 hours): day and night; clock time differing between places. Revolution (journey round the Sun in about 365¼ days): the seasons; days and nights of changing length.

etapes.action: Attack the false cause with a fact.
etapes.justification: A correct counter-fact is stronger than saying the statement is simply wrong.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, when the Northern Hemisphere has winter, so distance cannot explain the seasons.

etapes.action: Give the true cause in a chain.
etapes.justification: The explanation needs the tilt, the constant direction of the axis and the effect on the rays.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The axis is tilted by 23.5° and keeps its direction. In the northern summer, the Northern Hemisphere leans towards the Sun.

etapes.action: Finish with the consequence for both hemispheres.
etapes.justification: The seasons are opposite north and south, which shows the cause is the tilt and not distance.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The north gets direct rays and long days, so it is hot; the south leans away, gets slanting rays and short days, so it is cool.

sections.conclusion_markdown: Model answer: (a) Rotation causes day and night and differences in local time. Revolution causes the seasons and the changing length of day and night. (b) The student is wrong because the Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, when it is winter in the north. The seasons are caused by the 23.5° tilt of the axis, which keeps pointing in the same direction while the Earth revolves. In August the Northern Hemisphere still leans towards the Sun, receives more direct rays and longer days, and so has summer, while the Southern Hemisphere has winter.

items.erreur_markdown: "Rotation causes the seasons because the Earth keeps turning."
items.pourquoi_faux: Rotation takes about 24 hours and repeats every day. Seasons last for months, so they must come from a movement that takes a year.
items.correction_markdown: Rotation causes day and night. Revolution combined with the tilted axis causes the seasons.

items.erreur_markdown: "A solstice is the day when day and night are equal."
items.pourquoi_faux: Equal day and night describes an equinox. At a solstice the lengths are as unequal as they get.
items.correction_markdown: Solstice: overhead Sun at a tropic, longest day in one hemisphere and shortest in the other. Equinox: overhead Sun on the equator, day and night equal.

items.erreur_markdown: "The Earth's axis changes direction to follow the Sun during the year."
items.pourquoi_faux: If the axis followed the Sun there would be no seasons. It keeps pointing in the same direction in space, so the hemisphere facing the Sun changes as the Earth moves round its path.
items.correction_markdown: The axis is tilted by 23.5° and keeps its direction. This is why each hemisphere leans towards the Sun in turn.

items.erreur_markdown: "On 21 June it is summer all over the world."
items.pourquoi_faux: Seasons are opposite in the two hemispheres. When one leans towards the Sun the other leans away.
items.correction_markdown: On about 21 June the Northern Hemisphere has summer and the Southern Hemisphere has winter.

items.erreur_markdown: "Revolution takes exactly 365 days, so a calendar year never needs to change."
items.pourquoi_faux: The real time is about 365¼ days, so an extra day is added every fourth year to keep the calendar in step with the seasons.
items.correction_markdown: One extra day in four years gives a leap year of 366 days.

items.enonce_markdown: (a) Write one sentence defining a solstice and one defining an equinox. (b) At which latitude is the overhead Sun on about 22 December? (c) Which hemisphere has summer on that date?
items.solution_markdown: (a) **Solstice:** the date when the overhead Sun is at its furthest point from the equator, at the Tropic of Cancer or the Tropic of Capricorn, giving the longest day in one hemisphere and the shortest in the other. **Equinox:** the date when the overhead Sun is on the equator, so day and night are equal everywhere. (b) The Tropic of Capricorn, **23.5°S**. (c) The **Southern Hemisphere**, because it leans towards the Sun.

items.enonce_markdown: (a) The Earth turns through 360° in 24 hours. Through how many degrees does it turn in 6 hours? (b) A calendar year has 365 days, but the Earth takes about 365¼ days to go round the Sun. How many extra days build up in 12 years, and how many days do those 12 years contain once leap days are added?
items.solution_markdown: (a) Rate of turning = 360° ÷ 24 = 15° per hour. In 6 hours: 15° × 6 = **90°**. (b) Extra days = 12 × ¼ = 3 days, so 3 leap days are added. Total days = 12 × 365 + 3 = **4383 days**.

items.enonce_markdown: A school in a town at latitude 10°N studies the Sun at noon. (a) Give the latitude where the Sun is overhead on 21 June and on 21 December. (b) Work out the angle of the noon Sun above the horizon at the town on 21 June, on 21 December and at an equinox. (c) Explain in short points why the noon Sun at the town is highest on dates that are not solstices.
items.solution_markdown: (a) 21 June: 23.5°N. 21 December: 23.5°S. (b) Noon angle = 90° minus the number of degrees between the town and the overhead Sun. 21 June: 23.5° − 10° = 13.5°, so 90° − 13.5° = **76.5°**. 21 December: 10° + 23.5° = 33.5°, so 90° − 33.5° = **56.5°**. Equinox: the overhead Sun is on the equator, 10° away, so 90° − 10° = **80°**. (c) The overhead Sun moves between the two tropics because of the tilt and revolution. The noon Sun at the town is highest when the overhead Sun is exactly at 10°N, giving an angle of 90°. The overhead Sun crosses 10°N twice a year, once on its way north and once on its way south, and these dates fall between the equinoxes and the June solstice, not at the solstices. In December the overhead Sun is far away in the south, so the noon Sun is lowest. (Marks are given for naming the tilt, revolution, the moving overhead Sun and the idea of nearest latitude.)

items_markdown: Rotation (about 24 hours, west to east) gives day and night and differences in time. Revolution (about 365¼ days) with the tilted axis gives the seasons.
The axis is tilted by 23.5° and keeps the same direction in space. The distance from the Sun is not the cause: the Earth is closest to the Sun in early January.
Solstice: overhead Sun at a tropic, about 21 June and 22 December. Equinox: overhead Sun on the equator, about 21 March and 23 September, with equal day and night everywhere.
Seasons are opposite in the two hemispheres. Near the equator the length of day changes little during the year.
In a not-a-cause question, test each option against the tilt, the fixed direction of the axis and revolution.
